searchScope: All workbook course names, law-track codes, discipline and profile context considered; law/legal/recht/notarial/inheritance/estate/tax/property candidates inspected. All eight legal candidates already included in superseded proposal. No additional defining sequence established.

candidates.name: Transnational Business Law
candidates.description2: Businesses and entrepreneurs are confronted with legal complexity not only at the domestic level but particularly across divergent legal systems. This course presents a survey of the most essential fields of business law: contracts law, company law, trade law, intellectual property, and dispute resolution. An ultimate aim of the course is to critically examine the impact of globalization and digitization on the development of business law.
candidates.profile: This course introduces students to the legal frameworks governing business transactions in a globalized economy. It examines how law shapes cross-border trade, contracts, sales of goods and services, intellectual property, foreign investment, and digital commerce. Emphasis is placed on the practical application of legal rules to real-world business scenarios, as well as on comparative and international perspectives. Through interactive class discussions, problem - based assignments, quizzes, and an arbitration simulation, students develop the analytical and practical skills needed to identify legal risks and design effective solutions in transnational business contexts.
candidates.topics: business law; divergent legal systems; ultimate aim; dispute resolution; contracts law; intellectual property

candidates.name: Law, Society & Justice
candidates.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
candidates.profile: This course offers three different perspectives on the law: the legal, the social and the normative. We spend the first part of the course exploring the definitions of law and the different understandings of law in a general sense. We take a brief look at the different legal systems of the world, and we discuss various fields of law: constitutional law, administrative law, criminal law, international law and human rights, as well as select fields of private law including property law, contract and torts law. After the Fall break, students consider the relationships between law and society and the concept of justice. In addition to reading and discussing the main principles within each field of law, we explore these through reading case law and performing trial simulations.
candidates.topics: property law; torts law; moot court session; international legal organisations; legal traditions; socio scientific

candidates.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
candidates.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
candidates.profile: This course offers a broad approach to human rights: the legal, the historical and the theoretical/philosophical. In the first part of the course, human rights will mainly be studied in a legal way, adopting a legal perspective. Students will be introduced to the catalogue of human rights as positive law. Human rights treaties, the monitoring mechanisms and case law on human rights will be explored. This knowledge will be tested in a mid-term exam (multiple choice). In the second part, students will delve into a more historical and philosophical understanding of human rights. We will investigate the rise of the language of human rights in the 17th and 18th century, its culmination in the US Bill of Rights (1791) and the Déclaration des Droits de l’Homme et du Citoyen (1789). We will explore the further developments of the language in the 20th century in particular, which brought a great extension of the number and application of human rights. Students will read landmark cases that touch upon contentious, and often politicised disputes between liberty and equality. Some emphasis in this course will be given to natural law and its connection to human rights. We will delve into the classical and medieval scholarship on natural law, starting with Plato’s and Aquinas’ views on right and wrong. This will be compared to the modern views on the same going back to Hobbes and Locke, the latter considered to be the founding father of the rights paradigm. Human rights in today’s traditional societies will be investigated through selected case studies.
candidates.topics: human rights; french declaration; rights treaties; modern philosophers; traces; classical

candidates.name: Criminal Law & Criminal Justice
candidates.description2: Examines moral and legal justifications for criminalisation and punishment. Investigates guiding principles of criminal law and justice, including criminal accountability, guilt, legality and fundamental principles, and applies theory through a simulated legal aid clinic.
candidates.profile: This course provides students insights into the main legal issues in the fields of criminal law and criminal justice. We will discuss the concepts of criminal accountability, differentiated types of ‘guilt’, the essentials of justifications and excuse, the importance of the legality principle and other fundamental considerations, such as the ‘presumption of innocence’. Students are also introduced to interdisciplinary research into organized crime. The main guiding principles of criminal law and criminal justice will be presented and investigated and the moral and legal debate on the justification of punishment and on recent developments in criminal law will be considered. Special attention will be paid to legal skills, such as reading legal texts, analyzing criminal case law and formulating a normative opinion, based on legally and morally sound argumentation. Students apply theory and skills in a simulated legal aid clinic.
candidates.topics: ‘presumption of innocence’; reading legal texts; analyzing criminal case law; formulating a normative opinion; based on legally; morally sound argumentation

candidates.name: Introduction to Public International Law
candidates.description2: Introduces rules, institutions and politics of public international law. Covers treaties, the UN, armed conflict, war crimes, refugee protection and climate change. Students analyse cases, debate issues and produce a podcast connecting law to global challenges.
candidates.profile: This course serves as a general introduction to public international law as a field of study and professional discipline. Designed to provide you with a foundational knowledge of the creation and the historical evolution of the subject, it is broadly divided into three parts. The first part deals with general principles of international law such as its sources, subjects, and organization. In the second part, the focus shifts to specific domains, namely the regulation of the use of force, the law of armed co nflict, international criminal law, refugee law, and environmental law. The final part addresses the politics of international law as it delves into issues such as the right to self-determination, Third World Approaches to International Law, and questions of treaty negotiation, compliance and effectiveness. The general purpose of the course is to shed light on some of the most important questions of international law both from a formal legal and a social science perspective. Performance in the course will be assessed through in-class exercises, a preparatory and an open book exam, a podcast and a reflection report.
candidates.topics: its sources; right to self-determination; third world approaches to international law; questions of treaty negotiation; public international law; podcast connecting law

candidates.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
candidates.description2: Explores constitutional law and state organisation, using a comparative approach. Covers constitutionalism, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism and fundamental rights, and discusses constitution‑making, religious constitutions and constitutional backsliding.
candidates.profile: In this course on constitutional law and administrative law, students will undertake an exploration of the essential principles of these foundational legal fields. A comparative approach is used, examining and analyzing the constitutional law of five different legal systems. A constitution is the “fundamental and organic law of a nation or state that establishes the institutions and apparatus of government, defines the scope of governmental sovereign powers, and guarantees individual civil rights and civil liberties”, and ther efore, constitutional law is the “field of law dealing with aspects of constitutional provisions, such as restrictions on government powers and guarantees of rights.” (Blacks Law Dictionary 8 Ed, Garner et al eds, West 2004.) Yet, constitutional law is so much more than is suggested by these definitions. At the center of the modern constitutional state is the law, which protects peace, freedom and security. It is this law that is controlling, not the human actors in a state. In order that all may have acce ss to and rely on it, this law should be enshrined in a written document. Democracy demands a law that is enacted by a legislative body after public debate about its contents. The foundational values of a legal culture are written down in its constitution. The constitution takes up established values, tried and tested institutions and reliable political experience and passes them on to the next generation in a binding manner.
candidates.topics: restrictions on government powers; guarantees of rights; constitutional law; comparative; religious constitutions; judicial review

candidates.name: Principles of Private Law
candidates.description2: Examines principles of property law, tort law, contract law and other fields within private law. Uses comparisons of legal systems in four countries to explore rights and obligations arising from daily interactions.
candidates.profile: Life comprises a variety of situations in which private law plays a role . Simply considering the home implicates several complex relationships: family relatives , landlords and tenants, neighbors. Stepping out the front door leads to a further range of transactions that can have legal consequences for those involved. The rights and obligations associated with relationships and transactions among (natural and legal) persons are largely determined by a collection of legal areas known collectively as private law. This course introduces students to principles of selected fields of private law, and students will closely examine property law, tort law, contract law, and other legal areas. The overarching principles within each of these fields will be illuminated using a comparative law approach, considering primarily the legal systems of Germany, France, England, China, and the United States of America. Additionally, students will be challenged to consider private law concepts in broader contexts. Building on the skills acquired in GOSLAWJ101 and other UCR law track courses , this course on private law will seek to uncover the latent social, economic, and political pressures underlying many of the legal principles that will be discussed.
candidates.topics: latent social; private law; obligations arising; tort law; contract law; daily interactions

candidates.name: Foundations of European Union Law
candidates.description2: Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
candidates.profile: EU law is everywhere, from the very strict new rules on data-protection that literally pop-up with every website you open, to less apparent instances such as the EU rules on reducing plastic bags that have found their way into distinct and different national laws throughout the EU. European law by now significantly affects the legal order in European countries and reflects as well as shapes the process of European integration in multiple ways. This course introduces you to the EU legal order by familiarizing you first with the institutional framework of the European Union and the organization of its legal foundations in particular. We will then survey the key substantive areas of EU law that revolve around EU fundamental rights, citizenship, and the freedom of movement of persons, workers, goods and establishments. You will be equipped to understand the EU legal order and research its manifestations both at the EU level as well as in the domestic context in which most of the EU law manifests itself in the lives of citizens, consumers, businesses and governments. There will also be guest lectures to further illustrate EU law and its functioning in theory and practice. The course is divided in two main parts. In the first part we will jointly examine the procedural aspects of EU law through a combination of brief lectures, in-class exercises and discussions. In the second part we will study the substantive law of the EU through the method of Problem Based Learning. Students will study a relevant case using the seven-step PBL method.
candidates.topics: different national laws throughout the eu; problem based exercises; internal market; guest lectures; legal order; framework

conclusion: The workbook supports genuine comparative legal study: law and society, human rights, criminal justice, public international law, comparative constitutional/administrative law, private law and transnational business law. All eight law-focused courses together account for60EC in the proposed180EC programme. Principles of Private Law studies selected property, tort and contract principles primarily through Germany, France, England, China and the USA; Transnational Business Law addresses cross-border transactions, contracts, trade, intellectual property, investment, digital commerce and arbitration. Neither supplies the sustained Dutch property, inheritance, family/relationship-property, company and tax-law progression, notarial office law, civil/insolvency procedure and integrated Dutch legal research that define VU Notarieel Recht (OER10.3). The remaining120EC provide business, economics, statistics, rhetoric, negotiation and personal development. Accounting can support the business-economics element; negotiation and rhetoric can support communication. Public Economics studies taxation as economic policy, not Dutch tax doctrine; general research methods and market research do not supply the required independent notarial legal research. These are useful contributions but cannot replace the missing defining substance. A broader law/business/negotiation programme is a different target. The no-match conclusion concerns academic substance and weight, independently of professional eligibility or automatic master admission. A workbook-wide title/discipline/profile search found no additional notarial/property/inheritance/family/tax-law sequence from which to reconstruct a defensible response.

widerProfileMatches.name: Public Economics
widerProfileMatches.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
widerProfileMatches.profile: This course examines the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy affects efficiency and equity. It explores the rationale for government intervention and key concepts such as market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, p ublic spending, redistribution, and political economy. By combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, the course provides a framework for analysing the economic impact of public policies.

widerProfileMatches.name: Consumer Product Design
widerProfileMatches.description2: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.
widerProfileMatches.profile: In this course you will learn how to function in a 'real-world' design and development environment. Hence, you will work in a group that mimics a design and development (d&d) team as e.g. in industry. The members of a team in this course fulfill roles similarly as occur in industrial d&d teams (e.g. chair person, secretary, ...). A team is responsible for much of its own planning. The functioning of a team involves e.g. preparing agendas for team meetings, taking minutes, planning practical work, maintaining a documentation system, etc. During the course, the instructor will NOT act as chairperson / team leader, but rather as an ‘external consultant'. During the course we will go through the various phases of the development of a consumer product: assessment of customer needs and translating these into a product concept, develop a method to make a product, both on laboratory- as on industrial scale, analyzing environmental impact, analyzing costs and proceeds. In a d&d project and hence in the course, activities are quite varied, and include interviewing potential customers, laboratory experiments, constructing quantitative mathematical model(s) of the working mechanism(s) of a product, constructing a prototype, work out how a product can be produced on an industrial scale, consider protection of intellectual property etc.. In this course, in addition to the more traditional aspects of the d&d process, special attention will be given to sustainability. This involves e.g. the nature of the materials used (natural, recycled, …), lifespan, repairability, 'circularity' etc.
widerProfileMatches.topics: involves interviewing customers; probe customer needs; product; quantitative modeling; fabrication method; consumer

widerProfileMatches.name: Linear Systems
widerProfileMatches.description2: Focuses on analysis of linear systems from an engineering perspective. Explores representations via differential equations, transfer functions, state‑space and signal‑flow diagrams and discusses applications in control, signal processing and modelling.
widerProfileMatches.profile: The concepts of signals and systems appear in a wide variety of fields. The physical nature of the sig- nals to be acquired and the measurement systems may differ from application to application, but they all have in common that the signals contain information about the observed phenomenon and secondly, the systems respond to particular signals by producing other signals or certain behavior as output. This course discusses how to characterize alinear time-invariant systemand how it will respond to var- ious inputs. Theunit-impulse responseor - its equivalent in the frequency domain - thefrequency responsecharacterizes a linear time-invariant system. This course discussesconvolution. TheFourier series representationrepresents periodic signals as infinite harmonic series in continuous time and finite harmonic series in discrete time. Increasing the period of the periodic signals amounts to a denser Fourier series representation. In the limiting case that the period becomes infinitely long, the Fourier series rep- resentation becomes theFourier transform- both in continuous-time and in discrete-time. The course discusses the properties of the Fourier series representation and the Fourier transform in great detail. A very important characteristic of the Fourier transform is the duality property. TheLaplace transform generalizes the Fourier transform for continuous-time signals. In a very similar way, theZ-transform generalizes the Fourier transform for discrete-time signals.
widerProfileMatches.topics: signal flow diagrams; linear systems; state space; signal processing; transfer functions; differential equations

widerProfileMatches.name: Soils & Aquifers
widerProfileMatches.description2: Explores soils and aquifers through fieldwork and lab analyses. Covers soil formation, properties, health and remediation and investigates mapping aquifers for geothermal energy, coastal defence and freshwater resource assessment.
widerProfileMatches.profile: Explores soils and aquifers through fieldwork and lab analyses. Covers soil formation, properties, health and remediation and investigates mapping aquifers for geothermal energy, coastal defence and freshwater resource assessment.
widerProfileMatches.topics: soil formation; investigates mapping aquifers for geothermal energy; coastal defence; freshwater resource assessment; soils; covers soil

widerProfileMatches.name: Climate Change
widerProfileMatches.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
widerProfileMatches.profile: Climate change is the defining challenge of our time. It has large impacts on both the living and non-living Earth systems, as well as drives a number of profound societal transformations. This course is roughly divided in 3 parts. First, we will first focus on the drivers of anthropogenic climate change and its impacts on the natural world. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) the properties of greenhouse gases, sea level rise, ocean acidification, climate feedback loops and effects on various biome types. Secondly, we will discuss impacts on various aspects of society. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) food production, transportation, construction, health, and migration patterns. We will discuss climate governance and -justice. We will also look at the history of the climate change debate and identify strategies that have been deployed by interest groups to sow doubt and misinformation. Lastly, we will look into solutions for both adaptation and mitigation, such as renewable energy systems, carbon dioxide storage and climate-adaptive spatial planning. The course will include a number of guest lectures and excursions. After taking the course, you will be able to explain the fundamentals of climate change science. You will also be able to navigate a vast flow of information on climate change, and identify main and reliable sources; you will have insight in main climate change issues and have an overview of the pathways to mitigation and adaptation.
widerProfileMatches.topics: renewable energy systems; carbon dioxide storage; climate-adaptive spatial planning; anthropogenic climate change; ocean acidification; carbon storage

widerProfileMatches.name: Calling Bullshit
widerProfileMatches.description2: Develops skills to recognise and handle misinformation. Discusses cognitive biases and detection methods, distinguishes real from fake experts, and includes case studies and a video project tackling a misinformation topic.
widerProfileMatches.profile: The world is rife with misinformation. To function properly in any field, it is important that you are able to recognize it adequately handle it. In this course, you will develop your “bullshit-detector”. The course is structured around the following four questions: What is bullshit? The word “bullshit” is subject to a lot of philosophical essays, of which you will read some. It is important to get a clear view of what we mean by it, and what distinguishes it from lying, fake news, mis/disinformation, nonsense or baloney, false beliefs, or the slightly different “horseshit”. We will discuss this extensively in the first sessions. We will then proceed with a historical overview of misinformation and the role it played in politics and society as a whole. It is -kind of- reassuring that bullshit is nothing new: Fake news and smear campaigns can be traced back to Sumerian clay tablets and were prominent in Roman society (ask Mark Anthony!). Understanding the historical context enables us to recognize patterns. What makes us vulnerable to bullshit? We will discuss common biases in human thinking and social pressures that make us vulnerable to bullshit and other types of misinformation. We are all human, so everybody can fall victim to false beliefs. Understanding our own way of thinking and the way our social environment influences us, helps us to process information more reliably and sharpens our critical thinking skills. How can you recognize bullshit? You will learn how to detect and distinguish several types of bullshit using a taxonomy of bullshit.
widerProfileMatches.topics: misinformation; cognitive biases; fake news; pseudoscience; scientific credibility; critical thinking

widerProfileMatches.name: Biochemistry
widerProfileMatches.description2: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
widerProfileMatches.profile: Living organisms evolved from the prebiotic world through chemical reactions. Laws governing those early reactions are the same t oday. C hemistry is the underlying science behind biology. Biochemistry, the chemistry of life, deals with the reactions that produce the molecules of life: proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids that enable the self -assembly and reproduction of simple and complex organisms. Although organisms vary en ormously in complexity and biological properties, all domains of life use similar biomolecules for encoding and transmitting information, intra - and intercellular signaling, formation of membranes, building and degrading macromolecules, energy metabolism, and many more features. Errors in the production, proper localization or degradation of these molecules can often lead to disease. Biochemical knowledge is not only essential for understanding and treating these diseases, but also necessary for advancing many applications in biotechnology.
widerProfileMatches.topics: discusses metabolic pathways; nucleic acids; biomolecules; sugars; lipids; biotechnology

widerProfileMatches.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
widerProfileMatches.description2: Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.
widerProfileMatches.profile: This course covers a vast number of topics from general and molecular pathology and genetics of humans. The pathology portion includes the bases of pathology which is cell injury and cell death. The pathology also covers how acute and chronic inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration and fibrosis, and neoplasia contribute to pathologies. The course then shifts to understanding the molecular genetics underlying disease. The significance of chromosome structure and organization of genes will be covered along with gene mutations (and their inheritance) through several examples of genetic diseases. The course also focuses on the status of genetic testing and genetic treatments. Ethical and legal considerations for now and in the future will also be examined.
widerProfileMatches.topics: vast number of topics from general; molecular pathology; genetics of humans; how acute; chronic inflammation; tissue repair

widerProfileMatches.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
widerProfileMatches.description2: Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels.
widerProfileMatches.profile: Literature is common ground. It is ground not managed wholly by commercial interests, nor can it be strip-mined like popular culture…There’s a lot of talk about the tame world versus the wild world. It is not only a wild nature that we need as human beings; it is the untamed open space of our imaginations. Reading is where the wild things are. Jeannette Winterson Why Be Happy When You Can Be Normal. London, Vintage, 2012, p.144 The course is an introduction into practical criticism and literary interpretation. It explores some basic issues of literary study starting from the questions: what is literature, why do we read it, and why do we study it? The course familiarises students with formal properties of a literary work, makes them aware of a constructed character of literary text, and opens discussion of literary value. It is based on a classic division into three major genres (fiction, poetry and drama), supplemented by contemporary non-fiction, and rudiments of film narration. The goal of the course is to provide students with basic critical terms, tools and techniques that will make them sensitive readers and enhance their appreciation of a literary work.
widerProfileMatches.topics: romance novels; graphic narratives; film narration; non fiction; literary; interpret

widerProfileMatches.name: Media Archaeology
widerProfileMatches.description2: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
widerProfileMatches.profile: Media Archaeology explores the cultural and material significance of pre-digital media technologies, such as cassette tapes, typewriters, and early printed books, and how they shaped the production, circulation, and preservation of knowledge. We will study these objects from multiple perspectives, combining close material analysis with broader historical and cultural interpretation. You will examine how physical properties such as weight, texture, and durability influence communication and memory. The course will include seminar discussions, critical reflections, and hands-on activities that encourage active engagement with obsolete media. Practical exercises may involve recording silence, identifying the sonic characteristics of cassette hiss, or investigating the design, use, and cultural impact of the Sony Walkman. Through these activities, we will learn to treat media as both historical evidence and lived experience, linking material form to cultural meaning. These media objects are chosen because they exemplify the theories and readings central to debates in media archaeology today. By the end of the semester, you will have developed analytical thinking, interpretive skill, and cultural awareness consistent with the aims of a liberal arts education. You will be able to explain how studying obsolete and pre-digital technologies informs our understanding of today’s media. No technical expertise is required, only curiosity and a willingness to work closely with media as physical and cultural artifacts.
widerProfileMatches.topics: cassette tapes; early printed books; how they shaped the production; preservation of knowledge; durability influence communication; technical background required
